items.question: How is reducing-balance EMI calculated?
items.answer: Reducing-balance EMI uses the standard financial formula: EMI = [P × r × (1+r)^n] / [(1+r)^n - 1], where P is principal, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate / 12 / 100), and n is the tenure in months.

items.question: What is the difference between reducing balance and flat rate?
items.answer: In flat-rate loans, interest is charged on the original principal for the entire loan duration, resulting in a substantially higher effective interest cost compared to a reducing-balance loan of the same nominal rate.

items.question: How does the Indian Lakh / Crore numbering system work?
items.answer: When Indian Rupee (INR) is selected, figures are grouped in the South Asian format: 1,00,000 (1 Lakh) and 1,00,00,000 (1 Crore) using the en-IN formatting locale.

items.question: Can I download the month-by-month repayment schedule?
items.answer: Yes. You can export the complete repayment schedule as a CSV spreadsheet detailing principal, interest, and outstanding balance for every installment.

items.question: Does this calculator support 0% interest no-cost EMIs?
items.answer: Yes. If the interest rate is set to 0%, the monthly EMI simplifies exactly to Principal divided by tenure without division-by-zero errors.

items.question: Why is the final monthly EMI sometimes a few cents different?
items.answer: Because monthly payments are rounded to two decimal places, small fractional cent differences accumulate over decades. The final payment is adjusted to settle the remaining balance to exactly zero.

items.question: How does the principal-to-interest ratio change over time?
items.answer: Early payments consist primarily of interest charges because the outstanding principal balance is at its highest. As principal is paid down, subsequent interest charges shrink steadily.

items.question: How does this tool eliminate financial rounding errors?
items.answer: Every calculation is processed using decimal.js with half-up rounding, eliminating IEEE 754 floating point arithmetic inaccuracies.
